newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU agrees to limit nickel in euro coins.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees to limit nickel in euro coins.

text.p: European Union finance ministers, responding to consumer concerns about allergies, agreed on Sunday to limit the use of nickel in the euro coins which are planned to be in circulation by the year 2002.

A European Commission compromise proposal to include nickel in only two of the eight euro coins received the "preliminary" backing of all 15 EU countries, Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink told reporters.
The proposal by the EU executive also included various design features such as edgings to allow the blind to identify the money.
Sweden has been most critical of the use of nickel in the future European currency, arguing that it may cause allergies.
Asbrink welcomed the agreement, saying it was an important health and consumer issue, even though the country is set to remain outside economic and monetary union (EMU) from the 1999 start.
"This is a compromise," he said, adding that some countries had been reluctant but that in the end all backed the Commission's plan.

The European Consumers' Organisation (BEUC) has also lobbied to minimise the use of nickel in the new coins, saying there are "strong indications that nickel-containing coins may cause health problems at least to those who are already nickel sensitive and who have to handle the coins frequently."
Under Sunday's agreement, 92 percent of the euro coins would be nickel free compared to only 25 percent in today's national currencies.

A nickel-free alloy, Nordic gold, would be used for the 10, 20 and 50 cent coins and the one, two and five cent coins would also be nickel free. But with the current technology it would be difficult to develop an alternative to nickel for the one and two euro coins.
Nordic gold has no gold in it despite its name. It consists mainly of copper and is produced by Finnish metal group Outokumpu.
France is a major nickel producer through its New Caledonia territory in the South Pacific where the Eramet mining group is a large player.

Sweden's finance ministry has cited figures showing that 20 percent of young women in Europe are affected by nickel allergy, partly because of frequent exposure to the metal, for example by wearing earrings and other jewellery.

The ministers also discussed the designs of the face of the coins. Asbrink said there now seemed to be two alternatives and that the issue would be decided by EU leaders meeting in Amsterdam on June 16-17.

EU member states earlier decided in principle that the coins will have one common face showing a common subject and the value, and one face showing a national symbol surrounded by the 12 stars of the EU.
